headline: Estuary thermal engine carries the South Shore as the ocean stays unsettled
subhead: A 5-degree spread between the NY Bight at 57°F and the inside bay is stacking bass and bait on inlet structure and outgoing tide.
body_markdown:
The ocean off Fire Island is still wearing its spring coat. Buoy 44025 in the NY Bight is reading 57.0°F with 2.3-foot seas rolling on a 9-second dominant period out of the southeast, and the NY Harbor Entrance station (44065) is essentially the same water at 57.4°F with a northwest breeze around 12 knots gusting 16. Block Island offshore is colder yet at 56.1°F. Step inside any inlet on the South Shore, though, and the story changes — Kings Point on the Sound is already 58.6°F and Sandy Hook, the closest analog to our back-bay basins, is up to 63.1°F. That is the thermal architecture controlling every fish that matters this week: a cold, lumpy ocean pressed against a back bay that is climbing through the upper 50s and into the low 60s every time the sun gets on the mud.

What that delta means for this beat is simple. The bait — bunker schools that have been pushing through, plus the resident spearing and the squid still trickling along the beach — is sitting in the warm water. The bass and the early weakfish are sitting with the bait. The open ocean surf, with that southeast swell and a long-period roll, is fishable but not where the concentration is. The concentration is at the seams: the Fire Island Inlet throat, the sod banks behind Democrat Point, the rips under the Robert Moses bridges, and the mouths of the marsh creeks from Babylon east to Patchogue, where every outgoing tide pumps a slug of 60-degree water into the colder inlet column and rings the dinner bell.

The Captree night fishery has matured past the early-season clam grind. Clams will still produce on a slow drift on the dropping tide, but the better-quality fish are eating soft plastics worked along the channel edges between Sore Thumb and the West Bar — bass assassins, slug-gos, paddle-tails on a half-ounce to one-ounce head, fished slow on the swing. The class of fish reflects what is moving through the Bight right now: a heavy weighting toward slot and overslot bass, with comparatively few shorts, because we are inside the migratory pulse, not yet into the resident summer fish. Bluefish, the real ones in the eight-to-fifteen-pound class, have shown along the East End on hard current edges, and that wave is on the doorstep here — expect them on the Fire Island bars and at the inlet on the first hard ebb after a sunny afternoon.

Fluke have started but they are still a shallow-water story. With ocean bottom temperatures pinned in the mid-50s, the keeper grade fluke are inside — the flats off Captree, the channels between the islands east of Sexton, the drop into the West Channel. Bucktail-and-Gulp on a slow drift, 8 to 18 feet of water, is doing the work; the deeper Robert Moses ocean fluke drift needs another three to five degrees before it lights up the way it does in late June. Porgies are showing on the bay structure and around the bridges, blackfish season is closed, and weakfish reports remain sparse but the water is right for them in the deeper holes off Bay Shore and Nicoll Bay.

Looking three to five days out, the wind clocks matter more than anything. The current northwest flow is a friend — it flattens the inlet, keeps the bay clean, and lets the sun do its work on the flats. If we hold dry and sunny, the back bay pushes into the low 60s by midweek and the fluke bite expands east toward Patchogue. Watch for any east or southeast wind event, because at 2-foot seas with a 9-second period we are one bump away from a dirty, unfishable ocean front, and the bite will compress hard back inside the inlet. The new moon arrives June 5, so tides build steadily through the week — the bigger ebbs after dark are when I'd be on the bridges with plastics, and the bigger floods at first light are when the bait will push the bass up onto the Democrat Point bar.

This is a window where the inside angler wins. The ocean is the wrong temperature and the wrong sea state to bother with right now. Fish the thermal plume, fish the seam, fish the tide that carries warm water across cold, and let the migration come to you.
